Chapter 2: The Three Ego States — Parent, Adult, and Child.
Let’s take a closer look at why we interact the way we do.
Imagine you’ve got three different voices inside you, each ready to step up depending on what’s happening around you. These are called ego states—patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving that show up in response to certain situations.
And here’s the interesting part: everyone has three main ego states they draw upon—the Parent, the Adult, and the Child.
So, what exactly are these?
First, let’s talk about the Parent ego state. This is kind of like having an internal voice of authority—think of all those attitudes and rules you picked up from your parents, teachers, or other adults when you were growing up. Sometimes, this part of you is nurturing and supportive, offering comfort and guidance. Other times, it might sound critical, laying down the law or expressing disapproval. So, when someone’s being judgmental or giving advice you didn’t ask for, you can bet their Parent ego state is in charge.
Next up is the Adult ego state. This is the part of you that’s calm, rational, and focused on facts. It’s all about solving problems, making decisions based on what’s happening right now, and communicating clearly. Picture two people having a thoughtful, level-headed discussion—sharing ideas, weighing their options—that’s both of them operating from their Adult states.
And finally, there’s the Child ego state. This is where your emotions, creativity, and spontaneity live. It’s that playful, imaginative side that’s full of energy—but it can also be the part that feels scared, acts out, or craves approval. If you’ve ever seen someone sulk, throw a tantrum, or desperately seek reassurance, their Child ego state is probably running the show.
Now, here’s something important: these ego states aren’t separate personalities. They’re just different modes we all shift in and out of, sometimes in the same conversation! You might start by comforting a friend like a nurturing Parent, then switch to a logical Adult response, and finish off with a lighthearted, Childlike joke. Most of the time, these shifts happen automatically, shaped by both our past experiences and what’s going on in the moment.
So, why does it matter which ego state you’re in—or which one someone else is using? Well, recognizing these states can help you understand why certain interactions feel the way they do. For instance, if you’re in a heated argument, maybe one person is acting as a critical Parent, while the other is rebelling like a Child. On the other hand, when everyone’s working together calmly and focusing on solutions, they’re operating from their Adult states.
Getting a handle on ego states also helps you break patterns that aren’t working for you. Say you notice you slip into a Child role around authority figures—you can choose to switch gears and engage from your Adult state instead. That simple shift can change the whole dynamic, making conversations more balanced and respectful.
So, here’s the key takeaway: these three ego states—Parent, Adult, and Child—give you a simple, powerful way to understand the complexity of human relationships. By tuning in to which role you or others are playing, you can navigate any social situation with more insight and flexibility.
